entries.8c766a046f60319736adfb362472f124aa3eda09: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.4">2Sa 15:4</reference> <div eID="gen4451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4452" type="x-p"/> Absalom also said, <hi type="italic">“Oh that I might be judge in the land, and every one who had a cause might come before me; I would procure him justice!”</hi> ישׂמני מי is a wish: “who might (i.e., oh that one might) appoint me judge,” an analogous expression to יתּן ot מי (vid., Gesenius, §136, 1, and Ewald, §329, <hi type="italic">c</hi>.). עלי placed before יבא for the sake of emphasis, may be explained from the fact that a judge sat, so that the person who stood before him rose above him (comp. <reference osisRef="Exod.18.13">Exo 18:13</reference> with <reference osisRef="Gen.18.8">Gen 18:8</reference>). הצדּיק, to speak justly, or help to justice.
entries.ef8b961c12e41162d0375c3cd0a9be4cd753503a: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.5">2Sa 15:5</reference> <div eID="gen4452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4453" type="x-p"/> And when any one came near to him to prostrate himself before him, he took him by the hand and kissed him. It was by conduct of this kind that Agamemnon is said to have secured the command of the Grecian army (Euripid. <hi type="italic">Iphig. Aul.</hi> v. 337ff.).
entries.b321dae6e3f5d400aa8912751d98256056c2319f: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.6">2Sa 15:6</reference> <div eID="gen4453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4454" type="x-p"/> Thus Absalom stole the heart of the men of Israel. גּנּב לב does not mean to deceive or cheat, like לב גּנּב in the<hi type="italic">Kal </hi>in <reference osisRef="Gen.31.20">Gen 31:20</reference>, but to steal the heart, i.e., to bring a person over to his side secretly and by stratagem.
entries.0502b21fd487d02d5f378cb5c88da8a0acbab7f0: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.7-2Sam.15.8">2Sa 15:7-8</reference> <hi type="italic">Absalom’s rebellion.</hi> - <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.7">2Sa 15:7</reference>, 2Sa 15:8. After the lapse of forty (?) years Absalom said to the king, <hi type="italic">“Pray I will go</hi> (i.e., pray allow me to go) <hi type="italic">and perform a vow in Hebron which I vowed to the Lord during my stay at Geshur”</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.8">2Sa 15:8</reference>). The number forty is altogether unsuitable, as it cannot possibly be understood either as relating to the age of Absalom or to the year of David’s reign: for Absalom was born at Hebron after David had begun to reign, and David only reigned forty years and a half in all, and Absalom’s rebellion certainly did not take place in the last few weeks of his reign. It is quite as inappropriate to assume, as the <hi type="italic">terminus a quo</hi> of the forty years, either the commencement of Saul’s reign, as several of the Rabbins have done, as well as the author of the marginal note in <hi type="italic">Cod</hi>. 380 of De Rossi (שאול למלכות), or the anointing of David at Bethlehem, as Luther (in the marginal note) and Lightfoot do; for the word “after” evidently refers to some event in the life of Absalom, to which allusion has previously been made, namely, either to the time of his reconciliation with David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.14.33">2Sa 14:33</reference>), or (what is not so probable) to the period of his return from Geshur to Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Sam.14.23">2Sa 14:23</reference>). Consequently the reading adopted by the Syriac, Arabic, and Vulgate, also by <hi type="italic">Theodoret</hi> and others, viz., “<hi type="italic">four</hi> years,” must certainly be the correct one, and not “forty days,” which we find in Codd. 70 and 96 in Kennicott, since forty days would be far too short a time for maturing the rebellion. It is true, that with the reading ארבּע we should expect, as a rule, the plural שׁנים. At the same time, the numbers from two to ten are sometimes construed with a singular noun (e.g., 2Ki 22:1; cf. <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi>, §120, 2). The pretended vow was, that if Jehovah would bring him back to Jerusalem, he would serve Jehovah. את־יהוה עבד, “to do a service to Jehovah,” can only mean to offer a sacrifice, which is the explanation given by Josephus. The <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> ישׁיב is not the infinitive, but the imperfect <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi>: <hi type="italic">si reduxerit, reduxerit me</hi>, which is employed in an unusual manner instead of the <hi type="italic">inf. absol.</hi>, for the sake of emphasis. The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> ישׁוּב would have to be taken as an adverb “again;” but this is quite unnecessary.
entries.2af8c95a3179143a5da83958f1be23cf6cae67b2: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.9">2Sa 15:9</reference> <div eID="gen4454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4455" type="x-p"/> The king consented, and Absalom went to Hebron. Absalom had selected this city, probably assigning as the reason that he was born there, but really because his father David had been made king there, and also possibly because there may have been many persons there who had been displeased by the removal of the court to Jerusalem.
entries.17da5c7788686460240828a68edef637393441c7: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.10-2Sam.15.11">2Sa 15:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen4455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4456" type="x-p"/> When Absalom went to Hebron, he sent spies into all the tribes of Israel to say, <hi type="italic">“When ye hear the sound of the trumpet, say, Absalom has become king in Hebron.”</hi> We must suppose the sending the spies to have been contemporaneous with the removal of Absalom to Hebron, so that ויּשׁלח is used quite regularly, and there is no reason for translating it as a pluperfect. The messengers sent out are called “spies,” because they were first of all to ascertain the feelings of the people in the different tribes, and were only to execute their commission in places where they could reckon upon support. The conspiracy had hitherto been kept very secret, as we may see from the statement in <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.11">2Sa 15:11</reference> : <hi type="italic">“With Absalom there had gone two hundred men out of Jerusalem, invited </hi>(to the sacrificial festival),<hi type="italic">and going in their simplicity, who knew nothing at all of the affair.”</hi> (כּל־דּבר לא: nothing at all.)
entries.7359da04ac675b278ad920f62bc35607a2b79262: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.12">2Sa 15:12</reference> <div eID="gen4456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4457" type="x-p"/> Moreover, Absalom sent for Ahithophel, David’s councillor, to come from his own town Giloh, when he offered the sacrifices. The unusual construction of את ישׁלח with מעירו may be explained from the pregnant character of the expression: he sent and bade come, i.e., he summoned Ahithophel out of his city. <hi type="italic">Giloh</hi>, Ahithophel’s home, was upon the mountains of Judah, to the south or south-west of Hebron (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.51">Jos 15:51</reference>). Ahithophel had no doubt been previously initiated into Absalom’s plans, and had probably gone to his native city, merely that he might come to him with the greater ease; since his general place of abode, as king’s councillor, must have been in Jerusalem. <hi type="italic">“And the conspiracy became strong; for the people multiplied continually with Absalom”</hi> (the latter is a circumstantial clause). These words give a condensed summary of the result of the enterprise.
entries.4b2850cd600d80d501d8eece304d212d743df7b5: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.13-2Sam.15.14">2Sa 15:13-14</reference> <hi type="italic">David’s flight from Jerusalem.</hi> - <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.13">2Sa 15:13</reference>, 2Sa 15:14. When this intelligence reached David, <hi type="italic">“The heart of the men of Israel is after Absalom”</hi> (אהר היה, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.10">2Sa 2:10</reference>, to be attached to a person as king; see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.14">1Sa 12:14</reference>), he said to his servants that were with him in Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">“Arise, let us flee, for there will be no escape for us from Absalom! Make speed to depart, lest he overtake us suddenly, and drive the calamity</hi> (the judgment threatened in <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.10-2Sam.12.11">2Sa 12:10-11</reference>) <hi type="italic">over us, and smite the city with the edge of the sword.”</hi> David was perhaps afraid that Jerusalem might fall into Absalom’s power through treachery, and therefore resolved to fly as speedily as possible, not only in order to prevent a terrible massacre, but also to give his own faithful adherents time to assemble.
entries.67078891629530d7f0ef231df28d9c95ce9758d2: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.15-2Sam.15.16">2Sa 15:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen4457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4458" type="x-p"/> As his servants declared themselves ready to follow him, the king went out of the city with all his family in his train (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. at his feet, as in Jdg 4:10, Jdg 4:15, etc.), but left ten concubines behind to keep the palace.
entries.6dfd770b63d6ad1bdc8fad99f6924e664bdebfd3: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.17">2Sa 15:17</reference> <div eID="gen4458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4459" type="x-p"/> When outside the city the king and all the people in his suite (i.e., the royal family and their servants) halted at “the house of the distance.” המּרחק is probably a proper name given to a house in the neighbourhood of the city and on the road to Jericho, which was called “the farthest house,” viz., from the city.
entries.e8a2406121f8cdd9c9317d2109cc33f3142b3532: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.18">2Sa 15:18</reference> <div eID="gen4459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4460" type="x-p"/> And all his servants, i.e., his state officers and attendants, went along by his side, and the whole body-guard (the <hi type="italic">Crethi</hi> and <hi type="italic">Plethi</hi>: see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.18">2Sa 8:18</reference>); and all the Gathites, namely the six hundred men who had come in his train from Gath, went along in front of the king. David directed the fugitives to all into rank, the servants going by his side, and the body-guard and the six hundred old companions in arms, who probably also formed a kind of body-guard, marching in front. The verb עבר (passed on) cannot be understood as signifying to file past on account of its connection with על־ידו (beside him, or by his side). The expression <hi type="italic">Gittim</hi> is strange, as we cannot possibly think of actual Gathites or Philistines from Gath. The apposition (the six hundred men, etc.) shows clearly enough that the six hundred old companions in arms are intended, the men who gathered round David on his flight from Saul and emigrated with him to Gath (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.2-1Sam.27.3">1Sa 27:2-3</reference>), who afterwards lived with him in Ziklag (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.8">1Sa 27:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.2">1Sa 29:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.1">1Sa 30:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.9">1Sa 30:9</reference>), and eventually followed him to Hebron and Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Sam.2.3">2Sa 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.6">2Sa 5:6</reference>). In all probability they formed a separate company of well-tried veterans or a kind of body-guard in Jerusalem, and were commonly known as <hi type="italic">Gathites</hi>.<note placement="foot">The Septuagint also has πάντες οἱ Γεθαῖοι, and has generally rendered the Masoretic text correctly. But כּל־עבדיו has been translated incorrectly, or at all events in a manner likely to mislead, viz., πάντες οἱ παῖδες αὐτοῦ. But in the Septuagint text, as it has come down to us, another paraphrase has been interpolated into the literal translation, which Thenius would adopt as an emendation of the Hebrew text, notwithstanding the fact that the critical corruptness of the Alexandrian text must be obvious to every one.</note>
entries.a00e967fa539db0e2ff03093477079dd30974489: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.19">2Sa 15:19</reference> <div eID="gen4460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4461" type="x-p"/> A military commander named <hi type="italic">Ittai</hi>, who had emigrated from Gath and come over to David not long before, also accompanied the king from the city. It is evident from <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.2">2Sa 18:2</reference>, where Ittai is said to have commanded a third part of the army sent against Absalom, and to have been placed on an equality with Joab and Abishai the most experienced generals, that Ittai was a Philistian general who had entered David’s service. The reason for his going over to David is not known. According to <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.22">2Sa 15:22</reference> of this chapter, Ittai did not come alone, but brought all his family with him (<hi type="italic">taph</hi>: the little ones). The opinion expressed by Thenius, that he had come to Jerusalem as a hostage, is merely founded upon a false interpretation of the last two clauses of the verse before us. David said to Ittai, <hi type="italic">“Wherefore goest thou also with us? return and stay with the king; for thou art a stranger, and also emigrating to thy place.”</hi> There is no irony in the words “stay with the king,” as Thenius and Clericus suppose (viz., “with the man who behaves as if he were king”); nor is there an acknowledgment of Absalom as king, which certainly could never have emanated from David. The words contain nothing more than the simple though: Do you remain with whoever is or shall be king, since there is no necessity for you as a stranger to take sides at all. This is the explanation given by Seb. Schmidt: “It is not your place to decide this context as to who ought to be king; but you may remain quiet and see whom God shall appoint as king, and whether it be I or Absalom, you can serve the one that God shall choose.” This is the only way in which we can explain the reason assigned for the admonition, viz., “Thou art a stranger,” and not an Israelite. There is some difficulty connected with the following words (rendered in the Eng. version “and also an exile”). In the Septuagint and Vulgate they are rendered καὶ ὅτι μετώκησας σὺ ἐκ τοῦ τόπου σου, <hi type="italic">et egressus es de loco tuo</hi> (and thou hast gone out from thine own place); but in adopting this rendering the translators have not only passed over the גּם (also), but have taken למקומך for ממּקומך. Nevertheless Thenius proposes to bring the text into harmony with these versions for the purpose of bringing out the meaning, “and moreover thou art one carried away from his own home.” But this is decidedly a mistake; for David would never have made a Philistine - who had just before been carried away from his own home, or, as Thenius understands it, who had been brought to Jerusalem as a hostage - the commander of a third of his army. The meaning is rather the following: “And thou hast still no fatherland,” i.e., thou art still wandering about through the earth like an exile from his country: wherever thou findest a place, and art allowed to settle, there only canst thou dwell.
entries.2739875c4ef7057b796f24b0c0eed97a03a08302: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.20">2Sa 15:20</reference> <hi type="italic">“Thy coming is yesterday</hi> (from yesterday), <hi type="italic">and should I disturb thee to-day to go with us, when I am going just where I go?”</hi> i.e., wherever my way may lie (I go I know not whither; Chald.: cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.13">1Sa 23:13</reference>). The <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> אנוּעך is a copyist’s error. The thought requires the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> אניעך (<hi type="italic">Keri</hi>), as נוּע in the<hi type="italic">Kal </hi>has the intransitive meaning, to totter, sway about, or move hither and thither. <hi type="italic">“Return and take thy brethren back; grace and truth be with thee.”</hi> It is evidently more in accordance with the train of thought to separate עמּך from the previous clause and connect it with ואמת חסד, though this is opposed to the accents, than to adopt the adverbial interpretation, “take back thy brethren with thee in grace and truth,” as Maurer proposes. (For the thought itself, see <reference osisRef="Prov.3.3">Pro 3:3</reference>). The reference is to the grace and truth (faithfulness) of God, which David desired that Ittai should receive upon his way. In the Septuagint and Vulgate the passage is paraphrased thus: “Jehovah show thee grace and truth,” after <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.6">2Sa 2:6</reference>; but it by no means follows from this that עמּך ועשׂה והוה has fallen out of the Hebrew text.
entries.ff4b0ad6b900e35a802f81256a2ef4e1a77e0eed: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.21">2Sa 15:21</reference> <div eID="gen4461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4462" type="x-p"/> But Ittai replied with a solemn oath, <hi type="italic">“Assuredly at the place where my lord the king shall be</hi> (stay),<hi type="italic">whether for death or life, there will thy servant be.”</hi> אם כּי means “only,” as in <reference osisRef="Gen.40.14">Gen 40:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.42.8">Job 42:8</reference>; here, in a declaration on oath, it is equivalent to assuredly (vid., Ewald, §356, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.). The <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> is therefore correct, and the erasure of אם in the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> is a bad emendation. The כּי in the apodosis is either an emphatic declaration, <hi type="italic">yea</hi>, or like ὅτι merely introduces a distinct assertion. <div eID="gen4462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4463" type="x-p"/> After this assurance of his devotedness, David let Ittai do as he pleased. ועבר לך, “go and pass on.” עבר does not mean to pass by, but to go forward. Thus Ittai and his men and all his family that was with him went forward with the king. By “the little ones” (<hi type="italic">taph</hi>) we are to understand a man’s whole family, as in many other instances (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.12.37">Exo 12:37</reference>).
entries.a92dd88d01dfd32378cbf4e72ead87796528f029: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.22-2Sam.15.23">2Sa 15:22-23</reference> <hi type="italic">The king crosses the Kidron, and sends the priests back with the ark to Jerusalem.</hi> - 2Sa 15:23. All the land (as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.25">1Sa 14:25</reference>) wept aloud when all the people went forward; and the king went over the brook Kidron, and all the people went over in the direction of (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. in the face of) the way to the desert. The brook <hi type="italic">Kidron</hi> is a winter torrent, i.e., a mountain torrent which only flows during the heavy rains of winter (χείμαῤῥος τοῦ Κεδρών, Joh 18:1). It is on the eastern side of Jerusalem, between the city and the Mount of Olives, and derives its name from the appearance of the water when rendered muddy through the melting of the snow (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.6.16">Job 6:16</reference>). In summer it is nothing more than a dry channel in the valley of Jehoshaphat (see Robinson, <hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. i. 396, and v. Raumer, Pal. p. 309, note 81). <hi type="italic">“The wilderness”</hi> (<hi type="italic">midbar</hi>) is the northern part of the desert of Judah, through which the road to Jericho and the Jordan lay.
entries.993331dda62b1cb3211ba1708cb7827413392dae: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.24">2Sa 15:24</reference> <div eID="gen4463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4464" type="x-p"/> Zadok the priest and all the Levites (who were in Jerusalem) left the city with the fugitive king, bearing the ark of the covenant: <hi type="italic">“And they set down the ark of God, and Abiathar came up, till all the people had come completely over from the city.”</hi> ויּעל, ἀνέβη, <hi type="italic">ascendit</hi> (lxx, Vulg<hi type="italic">.</hi>), may probably be accounted for from the fact that Abiathar did not come to join the fugitives till the procession halted at the Mount of Olives; so that עלה, like ἀναβαίνειν, merely refers to his actually going up, and ויּעל affirms that Abiathar joined them until all the people from the city had arrived. The rendering proposed by Michaelis and Böttcher (“he offered sacrifices”) is precluded by the fact that עלה never means to sacrifice when written without עולה, or unless the context points distinctly to sacrifices, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.22">2Sa 24:22</reference>; 1Sa 2:28. The ark of the covenant was put down, because those who went out with the king made a halt, to give the people who were still coming time to join the procession.
entries.29dc51729e83381b0dba80e0cd1c6cb5a35109b7: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.25-2Sam.15.26">2Sa 15:25-26</reference> <div eID="gen4464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4465" type="x-p"/> Then the king said to Zadok, <hi type="italic">“Take back the ark of God into the city! If I find favour in the eyes of Jehovah, He will bring me back and let me see Him </hi>(i.e., himself: the reference is to God) <hi type="italic">and His dwelling</hi> (i.e., the ark of the covenant as the throne of the divine glory in the tent that had been set up for it). <hi type="italic">But if He thus say, I have not delight in thee; behold, here am I, let Him do to me as seemeth good to Him.”</hi> Thus David put his fate in believing confidence into the hand of the Lord, because he felt that it was the Lord who was chastising him for his sons through this rebellion.
entries.2b48e4bbfafc9f007fe044bd276b7e492bb333fd: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.27-2Sam.15.28">2Sa 15:27-28</reference> <div eID="gen4465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4466" type="x-p"/> He also said still further to Zadok, <hi type="italic">“Thou seer! return into the city in peace.”</hi> אתּה הרואה, with ה <hi type="italic">interrog</hi>., does not yield any appropriate sense, as ה cannot stand for הלוא here, simply because it does not relate to a thing which the person addressed could not deny. Consequently the word must be pointed thus, הראה (with the article), and rendered as a vocative, as it has been by Jerome and Luther. ראה, seer, is equivalent to prophet. He applies this epithet to Zadok, as the high priest who received divine revelations by means of the Urim. The meaning is, Thou Zadok art equal to a prophet; therefore thy proper place is in Jerusalem (O. v. Gerlach). Zadok was to stand as it were upon the watch there with Abiathar, and the sons of both to observe the events that occurred, and send him word through their sons into the plain of the Jordan. <hi type="italic">“Behold, I will tarry by the ferries of the desert, till a word comes from you to show me,”</hi> sc., what has taken place, or how the things shape themselves in Jerusalem. Instead of בּעברות, the earlier translators as well as the Masoretes adopted the reading בּערבות, “in the steppes of the desert.” The allusion in this case would be to the steppes of Jericho (2Ki 25:5). But Böttcher has very properly defended the <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> on the strength of <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.16">2Sa 17:16</reference>, where the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> has ערבות again, though עברות is the true reading (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.19">2Sa 19:19</reference>). The “ferries of the desert” are the places where the Jordan could be crossed, the fords of the Jordan (<reference osisRef="Josh.2.7">Jos 2:7</reference>; Jdg 3:28).
entries.d22581a23dbe5ea266b048a9bb5b738eed506395: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.29">2Sa 15:29</reference> <div eID="gen4466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4467" type="x-p"/> Zadok and Abiathar then returned to the city with the ark of God.
entries.e3ed8e5347bed5251b199a8f49c070472e54bbb1: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30-2Sam.15.31">2Sa 15:30-31</reference> <hi type="italic">Ahithophel and Hushai.</hi> - <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2Sa 15:30</reference>, 2Sa 15:31. When David was going by the height of the olive-trees, i.e., the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, with his head covered, and barefooted, as a sign of grief and mourning (see <reference osisRef="Esth.6.12">Est 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.17">Eze 24:17</reference>), and with the people who accompanied him also mourning, he received intelligence that Ahithophel (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.12">2Sa 15:12</reference>) was with Absalom, and among the conspirators. הגּיד ודוד gives no sense; for David cannot be the subject, because the next clause, “and David said,” etc., contains most distinctly an expression of David’s on receiving some information. Thenius would therefore alter הגּיד into the <hi type="italic">Hophal</hi> הגּד, whilst Ewald (§131, <hi type="italic">a</hi>) would change it into הגּיד, an unusual form of the <hi type="italic">Hophal</hi>, “David was informed,” according to the construction of the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> with the accusative. But although this construction of the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> is placed beyond all doubt by <reference osisRef="Job.31.37">Job 31:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.26.4">Job 26:4</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.10">Eze 43:10</reference>, the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> is construed as a rule, as the <hi type="italic">Hophal</hi> always is, with ל of the person who receives information. Consequently דּוד must be altered into לדוד, and הגּיד taken as impersonal, “they announced to David.” Upon receipt of this intelligence David prayed to the Lord, that He would “turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness,” make it appear as folly, i.e., frustrate it, - a prayer which God answered (vid., 2Sa 17:1.).
entries.4030cb380ba037c959a247483b517aa7dc4ffc03: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.32-2Sam.15.34">2Sa 15:32-34</reference> <div eID="gen4467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4468" type="x-p"/> On David’s arrival at the height where people were accustomed to worship, i.e., upon the top of the Mount of Olives, the Archite <hi type="italic">Hushai</hi> came to meet him with his clothes rent and earth upon his head, that is to say, in the deepest mourning (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.12">1Sa 4:12</reference>). It is evident from the words וגו אשׁר־ישׁתּחוה that there was a place of worship upon the top of the Mount of Olives, probably a <hi type="italic">bamah</hi>, such as continued to exist in different places throughout the land, even after the building of the temple. According to <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.37">2Sa 15:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.16">2Sa 16:16</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.33">1Ch 27:33</reference>, Hushai was רעה, a friend of David, i.e., one of his privy councillors. הארכּי (the Archite), if we may judge from <reference osisRef="Josh.16.2">Jos 16:2</reference>, was the name of a family whose possessions were upon the southern boundary of the tribe of Ephraim, between Bethel and Ataroth. <hi type="italic">Hushai</hi> was probably a very old man, as David said to him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.33">2Sa 15:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.34">2Sa 15:34</reference>), “If thou goest with me, thou wilt be a burden to me. But if thou returnest to the city and offerest Absalom thy services, thou canst bring for me the counsel of Ahithophel to nought. If thou sayest to Absalom, I will be thy servant, O king; servant of thy father (i.e., as regards this) I was that of old, but now I am thy servant.” The ו before אני introduces the apodosis both times (vid., Ewald, §348, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.).
entries.eef9a04b8cd95ad4c4f9e9e15afcc6e4988203e7: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.35-2Sam.15.36">2Sa 15:35-36</reference> <div eID="gen4468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4469" type="x-p"/> David then commissioned him to communicate to the priests Zadok and Abiathar all that he should hear of the king’s house, and send word to him through their sons.
entries.986f34497b4b626d61b314a5ca7d765c8dc82bcc: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.37">2Sa 15:37</reference> <div eID="gen4469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4470" type="x-p"/> So Hushai went into the city when Absalom came to Jerusalem. The רְְ before the second clause, followed by the imperfect יבוא, indicates contemporaneous occurrence (vid., Ewald, §346, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.).  <chapter eID="2Sam.15"/> <div eID="gen4470" type="x-p"/>

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="15" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>AND it came to pass after this, that Absalom <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 King. 1. 5.</ns0:note> prepared him charets, and horses, and fifty men to run before him <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">As being the Kings eldest Son, now <ns0:hi>Amnon</ns0:hi> was dead; for <ns0:hi>Chileab,</ns0:hi> who was his eldest Brother, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 3. 3. was either dead, or manifestly uncapable of the Government. And this course he knew would draw the eyes and minds of people to him, and make them conclude that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> intend<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed him for his Successor.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And Absalom rose up early <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Thereby making a shew of self-denial, and diligence, and solicitude for the good of the publick, and of every pri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vate person, as he had opportunity.</ns0:note>, and stood be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />side the way of the gate <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Either, First, Of the Kings Palace. Or rather, Secondly, Of the City, for that was the place of Judicature or <ns0:hi>Iudgment,</ns0:hi> for which these Men came.</ns0:note>: and it was <ns0:hi>so,</ns0:hi> that when any man that had a controversie, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> came to the king for judgment, then Absalom called un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to him <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Preventing him with the offers of his assi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stance.</ns0:note>, and said, Of what city <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> thou <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">As if he were ready to make particular enquiry into the state of his cause.</ns0:note>? And he said, Thy servant <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> of one of the tribes of Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rael <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Or rather, <ns0:hi>of one</ns0:hi> City (which word is easily understood out of the foregoing question) <ns0:hi>of the tribes of Israel,</ns0:hi> i. e. of an <ns0:hi>Israelitish</ns0:hi> City, either this, or that; of such or such a City.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And Absalom said unto him, See, thy matters <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> good and right <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Upon some very flight hearing of their case, he appro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved it, that he might oblige all.</ns0:note>: but <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> none will hear thee from the King <ns0:hi>downward.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> no man <ns0:hi>deputed</ns0:hi> of the king to hear thee <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">To wit, none such as will do thee Justice. The other Sons and Relations of the King, and the rest of the Judges and Rulers under him and them, are wholly corrupted, and swayed by favour or bribes; or, at least not careful and diligent as they should be: and my Father being grown in years, is negligent of publick affairs, leaving them wholly to their conduct.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Absalom said moreover, O that I were made judge in the land <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">For the King had onely restored <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> to favour, but thought not fit to put him into any place of Power and Trust.</ns0:note>, that every man <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">I should refuse no man, and decline no pains to do any man good. So he pretends to a very publick spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit.</ns0:note> which hath any suit or cause, might come unto me, and I would do him justice.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And it was <ns0:hi>so,</ns0:hi> that when any man came
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:259" />
nigh <ns0:hi>to him,</ns0:hi> to do him obeisance, he put forth his hand, and took him and kissed him <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Putting on the Garb of singular humanity and good will to all men. For that seems to have been a Ceremony, in frequent use in those times, of shewing respect, as pulling off the hat, and bowing, or imbracing, is at this day with us.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And on this manner did Absalom to all Israel, that came to the king for judgment: so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He secretly and subrilly undermined his Father, and robbed his Father of the good opinions and affections of his people, that he might gain them to himself, by such insinuations into their affections, by his plausible and over<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />civil carriage.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 ¶ And it came to pass after forty years <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> Whence are these to be computed? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Not from <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s Birth; for he was Born in <ns0:hi>Hebron</ns0:hi> some considerable time after <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had begun his Reign, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 3. 3. much less from the time of his Vow made, or of his return from Banishment: but, either, first, from the time of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s election or designation to the Kingdom, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 16. 13. Or, Secondly, From the beginning of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Reign: which being a Solemn time, and observable for the change of the Government in <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> might very fitly be made an <ns0:hi>Epocha,</ns0:hi> from which the computation or account of times begin; as the <ns0:hi>Greeks</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> began their accounts in the same manner, and upon the same ground. Or rather, Thirdly, From the beginning of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Reign, who Reign<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed 40 Years; and so the words may be rendred, <ns0:hi>about</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>towards the end of forty years,</ns0:hi> i. e. in the beginning of the fortieth Year. And so this very Phrase is used, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 15. 1. <ns0:hi>At the end of every seven years,</ns0:hi> i. e. in the seventh Year, even from the beginning of it, as is manifest and confessed. So in a like expression, <ns0:hi>After three days will I rise again, Mark</ns0:hi> 8. 31. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> on the beginning of the third day, when Christ did rise; the number of three days being then com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pleated when the third day is begun. And the 40 Years are here expressed as one motive or inducement to <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> to Rebel, because now his Fathers end grew near; and one of the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Doctors affirms, that there was a tradition, or rumour, or prediction, that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> should Reign but 40 Years. And <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> might easily understand that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> intended to decline him, and to make <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> his Successor, as well by the conscience of his own wickedness and unfitness for so great a trust, as by that eminent Wisdom and Piety which appeared in <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> in his tender Years, and that great re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spect and affection which his Father must needs have and manifest to him upon this account, and by that Promise and Oath given to <ns0:hi>Bathsheba</ns0:hi> concerning his Succession mention<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 1. 30. but made before that time, which also might come to <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s ear. Against this opinion two things are Objected: First, That <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> was in the time of this Rebellion a strong Man, for he Marched on Foot, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 30. whereas in his last Year he was very infirm and bed-rid. Se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />condly, That after this Rebellion was ended, divers other things happened, as the three Years Famine, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 21. 1. and other things following in the History. But it may be Answered to the first, That <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> might in the beginning of his last Year, have so much strength and vigour left as to March on Foot, especially when he did so humble and af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />flict himself, as it is apparent he did, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 30. and yet through his tedious Marches, and the tormenting Cares, Fears, and Griess of his Soul for <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> might be so strangely and suddenly impaired, as in the end of the same Year to be ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry feeble and bed-rid, it being a very common accident, especially in old Men, and upon extraordinary occasions, to languish and decline exceedingly, and to fall from some competent degree of health and vigour, to be very infirm and bed-rid, and that in the space of a few Months. And to the second Objection, That those Histories related <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 21, &c. though they be placed after this Rebellion, yet indeed were done before it; the proof of which see on <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 21. 1. For it is so confessed and evident, that things are not always placed in the same order in which they were done, that it is a Rule of the <ns0:hi>Hebrews,</ns0:hi> and approved by other Learned men, <ns0:hi>Non <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> prius & posterius in Sacris literis,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>There is no first and last in the order of Scripture relations.</ns0:hi> And here is a plain reason for this transplacing of this History, which is allowed in other like cases, That when once the Hi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />story of <ns0:hi>Tamar</ns0:hi>'s Rape had been mentioned, it was very fit to subjoin the Relation of all the Mischiefs which followed upon that occasion. If any Infidel will yet cavil with this Text and number of Years, let him know, that instead of <ns0:hi>forty,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Syriack,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Arabick,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iosephus</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Iew,</ns0:hi> read <ns0:hi>four years;</ns0:hi> and that it is much more rational to acknowledge an Error of the Scribe, who Copied out the Sacred Text, than upon so frivolous a ground to question the Divine Authority of the Holy Scriptures. And that some men chuse the latter way rather than the former, is an evidence that they are In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fidels by the choice of their wills, more than by the strength of their reasons.</ns0:note>, that Absalom said unto the king, I pray thee, let me go, and pay my vow <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">He pretends Piety, which he knew would please his Father, and easily procure his consent.</ns0:note> which I have vowed unto the LORD in Hebron <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Which is mentioned as the place, not where the Vow was made, for that was at <ns0:hi>Geshur, v.</ns0:hi> 8. but where he intended to per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />form it. The pretence for which was, That he was Born in this place, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 3. 3. and that here was a famous high-place; and, till the Temple was built, it was permit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted to Sacrifice upon the high-places.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 For thy servant vowed a vow while I abode at Geshur in Syria, saying, If the LORD shall bring me again indeed to Jerusalem, then I will serve the LORD <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Worship him by the offering of Sacrifices of Thanksgiving to God for restoring me to the place of his pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sence and service, and to my Fathers favour. But why should not this service have been performed at <ns0:hi>Sion,</ns0:hi> or at <ns0:hi>Gibeon?</ns0:hi> Here was some ground of suspition; but God blinded <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s eyes, that he might bring upon <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and upon <ns0:hi>Ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />salom</ns0:hi> the Judgments which they deserved, and he designed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And the king said unto him, Go in peace. So he arose, and went to Hebron <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">This place he chose as being an eminent Ciry, and next to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> the chief of the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> and the place of his Birth, and the place where his Father began his King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom, which he took for a good omen, and where it is pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bable that he had secured many Friends, and which was at some convenient distance from <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> that his Father could not suddenly reach him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 ¶ But Absalom sent <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">From <ns0:hi>Hebron.</ns0:hi> Or, <ns0:hi>had sent</ns0:hi> from <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> that when he went to <ns0:hi>Hebron,</ns0:hi> they should go into the several Tribes to sift the people, and to dispose them to <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s party, and acquaint them with his success.</ns0:note> spies throughout all the Tribes of Israel, saying, Assoon as ye hear the sound of the trumpet <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Which I shall take care to have sounded in several parts by other persons; and when that is done, you shall inform them of the reason of it. Or, as soon as you understand that the Trumpet was Sounded at <ns0:hi>Hebron;</ns0:hi> partly, to call the people together for my assistance; and partly, to celebrate my Inauguration to the Kingdom, which you shall speedily know by messengers whom I shall send to you to that end.</ns0:note>, then ye shall say, Absalom reigneth in Hebron.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And with Absalom went two hundred men out of Jerusalem, <ns0:hi>that were</ns0:hi> called <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Such as <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> had pick't out as fit for his purpose, such as were of some quality and reputation with the King and people, which would give a great countenance to his un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dertaking, and give occasion to people at first to think that this was done by his Fathers consent or connivence, as being now aged, and infirm, and willing to resign the Kingdom to him, as his eldest Son, and the Noblest too, as being de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />scended from a King by both Parents; and such as by their wisdom and interest in the people, might have done <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> much service in thiis needful time; yet such as were not very Martial men, nor likely with violence to oppose his pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceedings.</ns0:note>, and they went in their simplicity, and they knew not any thing <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Concerning <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s design.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nite <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Who is thought to have been the Author, or, at least, the fomenter of this Rebellion; either, because he was discon<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tented with <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> for which there might be many reasons; or, because he saw the Father was old and nigh his end, and he thought it best policy to worship the rising Sun, and to follow the young Prince, whom he observed to have so great an interest in the hearts of the people, and whom he supposed he could easily manage as he pleased, which he could not do with <ns0:hi>David.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, Davids Counsellor, from his city, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> from Giloh, while he offered sacrifices <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Which he did not in Devotion to God, for he neither feared God, nor reverenced Man; nor to implore Gods favour and assistance against his Father, which he knew was a vain thing to expect; but meerly that upon this pretence he might call great numbers of the people to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gether, whereof many would come to join with him in the Worship of God, and most to partake of the Feasts which were made of the remainders of the Sacrifices, according to the manner.</ns0:note>: and the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spiracy was strong, for the people increased con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinually with Absalom.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:260" />13 <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> And there came a messenger to David, saying, The hearts of the men of Israel are after Absalom<ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The generality of the people are for him. Which is not strange, considering, either, first, <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> whose many mis<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>arriages had greatly lost him in the hearts of his peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple. Or, Secondly, The people, whose temper is generally unstable, weary of old things, and desirous of changes, and apt to expect great benefits thereby. Or, Thirdly, <ns0:hi>Absa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lom,</ns0:hi> whose noble Birth, and singular Beauty, and most obliging Carriage, and ample Promises, had won the peoples hearts, considering also that he was <ns0:hi>David's</ns0:hi> first-born, to whom the Kingdom of right belonged, and yet that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> intended to give away his right to <ns0:hi>Solomon,</ns0:hi> which the people thought might prove the occasion of a civil and dreadful War, which hereby they designed to prevent. Or, Fourthly, The Just and Holy God, who ordered and over-ruled all these things for <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s chastisement, and the instruction and ter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ror of sinners in all future Ages.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And David said unto all his servants, that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him at Jerusalem, Arise, and let us flee<ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">For though the Fort of <ns0:hi>Zion</ns0:hi> was strong and impregna<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble, and he might have defended himself there; yet he had not laid in provisions for a long Siege; and, if he had been once besieged there, <ns0:hi>Absal<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>m</ns0:hi> would have got speedy and quiet possession of his whole Kingdom; whereas if he Marched a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />broad, he might raise a considerable Army for his defence and the suppression of the Rebels. Besides, the greatest part of <ns0:hi>Ie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rusalem</ns0:hi> could not be well defended against him. And he suspe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cted that a great number of the Citizens might take part with <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> and possibly deliver him up into <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s hand's. Besides, if he had made that the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>eat of the War, he feared the destruction of that City, which he vehemently desired to preserve, because it was the Chief and Royal City, and the place in which God had appointed to put his Name and Worship. Moreover, when <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> considered, that Gods hand was now against him, and that he was now bringing <ns0:hi>evil upon him out of his own house,</ns0:hi> as he had threatned, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 12. 11. it is no wonder if he was intimidated and disposed to flee.</ns0:note>: for we shall not <ns0:hi>else</ns0:hi> escape from Absalom: make speed to depart, le<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t he overtake us suddenly, and<ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> thrust.</ns0:note> bring evil upon us, and smite the city with the edge of the sword.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And the kings servants said unto the king, Behold, thy servants <ns0:hi>are ready to do</ns0:hi> whatsoever my lord the king shall<ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> chuse.</ns0:note> appoint.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And<ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 3. title.</ns0:note> the king went forth, and all his houshold<ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> at his feet.</ns0:note> after him<ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>on foot,</ns0:hi> by comparing <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 30. which the King chose to do, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ather than to ride; partly, to humble himself under the hand of God; partly to encourage his companion<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> in this hand and comfortless March; and partly, to move com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />passion in his people towards him.</ns0:note>: and the king left ten women <ns0:hi>which were</ns0:hi> concubines<ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">For he supposed that their Sex would protect them even among <ns0:hi>Barbarians,</ns0:hi> and their relation to <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> would gain them some respect, and, at least, safety from his Son.                   <ns0:p n="17">17 And the king went forth, and all the people after him, and tarried<ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Either to rest and refresh themselves a little: or rather in expectation of others who should or would come after him, that they might March away in a considerable Body, which might both defend the King, and invite others to come in to their assistance.</ns0:note> in a place that was far off<ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">At some convenient distance, but not very far.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
